read_this_first: Like for like: the 40 QuixBugs bugs the tree's own repair solver was measured on, the same tests deciding, about the same number of test runs per bug.
The tree's repair solver, not edited: 5 of 40 repaired with nothing taught, 6 with every other published fix taught first (canonical/verification/QUIXBUGS_REPAIR_SOLVER_20261111_V1.json).
The edit-kind learner shown the 164 HumanEvalFix fixes and no QuixBugs fix at all: 20 of 40 repaired; 10 are the published fix. Shown the other 39 QuixBugs fixes as well: 21 of 40.
Bug by bug against the solver with nothing taught: both 4, the learner alone 16, the solver alone 1, neither 19.

The 10 repairs that are not the published fix were READ, not run on further inputs: 1 not judged, 1 the same answers, 1 the same answers, slower, 5 the same behaviour, 2 wrong in general. A program that passes its tests is not therefore right.

Not a score on unseen bugs: all 40 QuixBugs fixes were read earlier in this work, and the learner's limit of 300 candidates per operator was chosen with QuixBugs timings in view. The lessons of the first line (HumanEvalFix only) contain no QuixBugs fix.
One run, one machine, by the producer. Nobody else has re-run it.

removed: return any((search_from(nextnode) for nextnode in node.successors))
put_in: return any((search_from(goalnode) for nextnode in node.successors))

depth_first_search.why: search_from(goalnode) is asked for every successor, which is true at once: any node with a successor "reaches" the goal

find_first_in_sorted.why: while lo + 1 <= hi is while lo < hi, the published fix

get_factors.why: the loop runs up to n instead of its square root, so a prime is found as its own factor; the published fix returns [n] at the end

is_valid_parenthesization.why: return depth % 4 == 0 and True: four unclosed brackets count as valid; the published fix is return depth == 0

lcs_length.why: dp[i, j + 1] = dp[i - 1, j] + 1 is the published recurrence with j moved by one; the answer is the largest value

levenshtein.why: 1 - 1 + levenshtein(...) is levenshtein(...), the published fix

minimum_spanning_tree.why: the loop runs over the group of u instead of the group of v; whether that is always right was not worked out

next_permutation.why: perm[j] > perm[i] is perm[i] < perm[j], the published fix

removed: lesser = quicksort([x for x in arr[1:] if x < pivot])
put_in: lesser = quicksort([x for x in arr[1:] if x <= pivot])

quicksort.why: equal elements go to the lesser side instead of the greater side

removed: return {'+': lambda a, b: a + b, '-': lambda a, b: a - b, '*': lambda a, b: a * b, '/': lambda a, b: a / b}[symbol](a, b)
put_in: return {'+': lambda a, b: a + b, '-': lambda a, b: a - b, '*': lambda a, b: a * b, '/': lambda a, b: a / b}[symbol](b, a)

rpn_eval.why: the two operands change places, as in the published fix

limits: QuixBugs has no second set of inputs; the repairs that differ from the published fix were judged by reading only.
The solver's 5 repairs were judged the same way in its own record: 2 are the published fix.
One bug (levenshtein) could not go through the confined screen (its buggy program does not end in time there) and was asked through the benchmark's own runner with a budget of 150 candidates.
A candidate has 1.5 seconds per wave in the screen; three buggy programs never end (bitcount, find_first_in_sorted, sqrt), so most of their candidates cost that long.
The comparison is on tests passed with about a thousand test runs per bug on both sides; the solver stops at its own bounds, the learner at 1000 candidates.
